key_facts: **Fixed drug eruption (FDE)** recurs at the **same site** each time the culprit drug is taken.
Round dusky red-purple patch, sometimes blistering, within hours; lips, genitals, hands, face; leaves grey-brown pigmentation.
Culprits: NSAIDs, paracetamol, co-trimoxazole, tetracyclines, laxatives (phenolphthalein historically).
Stop and avoid the drug; record the allergy; potent topical steroid for a few days.
Generalised bullous FDE can mimic SJS/TEN: urgent assessment.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: A drug reaction that **recurs at exactly the same site(s)** each time the drug is taken. Usually there are one or a few round, dusky-violet plaques, leaving **slate-brown/grey pigmentation**.

sub: Any age; often over-the-counter painkillers; recurrent episodes before diagnosis.

ul: Intermittent use of a drug, often OTC.
**"It's an infection like herpes"**: recurrence at the same site after a drug points to FDE (genital FDE is often mistaken for HSV).

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: FDE is caused by **memory T cells that stay in the skin** at the original site.

mech.t: The drug triggers CD8+ T cells that attack keratinocytes at one site.
Some CD8+ T cells remain in the epidermis of that patch long-term.
mech.caption: Fixed drug eruption: memory T cells resting at the site (left) are reactivated by the drug, causing interface damage, a blister and a dusky patch (right).

mech.t: Each dose reactivates them within hours, causing a dusky patch, sometimes with blistering.
Damaged basal cells drop melanin into the dermis, leaving persistent brown-grey pigment.

blocks: **Intraepidermal CD8+ tissue-resident memory T cells** persist at the original site. On re-exposure they activate within hours and release IFN-γ and granzymes → localised keratinocyte death (type IVc, like a "mini-TEN"). Melanin dropping into the dermis gives the persistent pigment.

**Common culprits:** **NSAIDs** (diclofenac, ibuprofen, naproxen, **mefenamic acid** — note the menstrual link), **co-trimoxazole/sulfonamides**, **tetracyclines**, **paracetamol**, metronidazole, fluconazole, barbiturates, carbamazepine, **sildenafil** (genital), antihistamines (cetirizine, hydroxyzine), quinine (in tonic water), phenolphthalein (old laxatives) and food dyes.

histo: Interface dermatitis with necrotic keratinocytes and pigment incontinence; eosinophils.

ul: **Lips**, **genitals** (glans penis), hands, feet, face; the trunk and limbs less often.
Round/oval, sharply demarcated, **dusky red-violet plaques**, often with a darker/targetoid or bullous centre. Burning or itch appears **30 min–8 h** (up to 48 h) after a dose.
Each recurrence may add **new sites**. Lesions resolve over 1–3 weeks with **post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation**, which is especially marked in skin of colour.
**Generalised bullous FDE (GBFDE):** multiple large blistering plaques (>10% BSA) in older patients. It mimics SJS/TEN, carries significant mortality (~20%) and **needs admission**.

**The case:** a 26-year-old with a **pigmented patch on the upper lip**, after **diclofenac during two consecutive periods**. Erythema/blistering recurring at the same site, then pigmentation → **FDE (diclofenac)**. It had been treated as a **cold sore**.
History of **recurrence at the same site** after intermittent drug use (menstrual NSAIDs, weekend antibiotics, "headache tablets") — ask specifically about intermittent OTC products.
Biopsy if doubtful (interface dermatitis, necrotic keratinocytes, dermal melanophages).
**Lesional patch test** (drug applied to the old site) or supervised **oral provocation** in specialist settings. Not for GBFDE.

sections.title: Differential diagnoses
blocks: Also: lichen planus pigmentosus, Bowen's disease (fixed, but persistent), bullous pemphigoid, SJS/TEN (vs GBFDE).

sections.title: Management

ol: **Stop and avoid diclofenac.** Record "**diclofenac — fixed drug eruption (lip)**", and inform her that structurally related NSAIDs (acetic-acid group: aceclofenac, indometacin, etodolac) may cross-react. Some patients tolerate structurally unrelated NSAIDs, but cross-reactivity is unpredictable — specialist advice before a trial.

**Dysmenorrhoea alternatives:** **paracetamol**, local heat, a hormonal method (COC/LNG-IUS/desogestrel) that suppresses ovulation/pain, TENS. Consider gynaecology review if dysmenorrhoea is severe (endometriosis).

**Acute lesion:** potent topical steroid for a few days (a moderate steroid on the lip, short course), emollient/lip balm; for erosions, non-adherent care. The pigmentation fades slowly (months), and more slowly with repeated exposure — sun protection helps.
**Check OTC purchases** (diclofenac gel, combination cold remedies, mefenamic acid) and tell her community pharmacy. Yellow Card (FDE is reportable, especially if bullous).

blocks: Fully within IP scope (recognition, stopping the drug, alternative analgesia/contraception, topical steroid, documentation, Yellow Card). Provocation testing is specialist.

refer.t: Many or widespread blistering patches, mucosal involvement or an unwell patient: possible **generalised bullous FDE**, same-day assessment.
A 'cold sore' that always appears after the same tablet: ask about over-the-counter NSAIDs and paracetamol combinations.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Many or widespread blistering patches, mucosal involvement or an unwell patient: possible **generalised bullous FDE**, same-day assessment.
A 'cold sore' that always appears after the same tablet: ask about over-the-counter NSAIDs and paracetamol combinations.

blocks: Multiple/generalised blistering plaques (GBFDE → same-day admission); mucosal erosions beyond the lip; uncertain diagnosis (genital lesions — exclude STI/HSV).

ul: Persistent pigmentation; generalised bullous FDE (rare, serious).
Does not recur if the drug is avoided; pigment fades slowly.

pearls: "**Same place, same drug, every time.**" Ask what she took in the 24 h before each flare.
A "cold sore" that leaves a **dark patch** and no vesicles is FDE until proven otherwise.
Menstrual NSAIDs are a classic hidden culprit; so are the "weekend antibiotics" for UTIs (co-trimoxazole/trimethoprim).

quiz.q: When should you think of Fixed drug eruption?
quiz.a: A round, dusky red-brown patch on the lip, genitals, hands or face that recurs at the same site, often mistaken for a cold sore.
Memory T cells sitting in the skin at that site are reactivated by the drug within hours.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Find the intermittent drug (ask about period pain relief, cold remedies, laxatives); stop and avoid it; potent topical steroid; document.
Generalised bullous FDE, which can resemble SJS/TEN and needs same-day assessment.

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: Many or widespread blistering patches, mucosal involvement or an unwell patient: possible **generalised bullous FDE**, same-day assessment.
